item.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
item.description: Stanford Events — The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future. The exhibition explores Kim’s concept of “Indigenous Futures” through art as a form of civilizational transformation, expressing p'owŏl (포월 抱越), embracing and transcending the pain and contradictions of reality while reaching toward new possibilities for the future. The opening reception on October 8 will feature an artist talk and a Korean mask dance (탈춤 t'alch'um) performance by Kim Bong-Jun and Che Se-hyun, a Seattle-based creative director and multidisciplinary artist. item.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
item.description: Stanford Events — Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day. The exhibition includes microscope images revealing the textile structure of the woven text as well as a woven enlargement that illustrates its basic principles, along with several artworks inspired by or related to the themes of the exhibition. Location: Green Library, Bing Wing

item.title: Electric Contrasts: the Art of the Detail
item.description: Stanford Events — Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century. The exhibition reveals the anachronistic and provocative juxtapositions of artworks in avant-garde magazines and books which created a radically new vision that would go on to influence television and the internet. Curated by Altair Brandon-Salmon. Bowes Art & Architecture Library hours: M-Th 9-7pm; Friday 9-5pm; Sunday 12-6pm. Tour by Dr. Brandon-Salmon on 9/5 at 6 pm prior to Electric Contrasts Study Evening. Location: McMurtry Building

item.title: A Vision of Paris: The Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford
item.description: Stanford Events — Stanford University Libraries presents A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford, on view in the Peterson Gallery and Munger Rotunda of the Cecil H. Green Library from September 22, 2026 to January 24, 2027. Roxane Debuisson (1927–2018) dedicated sixty years to documenting the transformation of the city of Paris during the nineteenth century. If Roxane Debuisson could not stop the changes she saw underway in the late 20th century, she could at least preserve the city’s earlier history through images, literature, guidebooks, and other documents. Her lifelong project helped to document Paris during the nineteenth century, especially the city’s rapid changes from the 1850s to the 1870s, when Emperor Napoleon III and his prefect of the Seine, Baron Eugène Haussmann, transformed the city with new boulevards, green spaces, and public utilities, and fostered innovations in commercial and cultural practices. item.title: Planetary Science and Exploration Seminar, Barron Nguyen / Alexis Hensley
item.description: Stanford Events — Barron Nguyen NSF Graduate Research Fellow / Coterminal M.S. student in Earth and Planetary Sciences, Stanford University Recent JWST Insights into Rocky Planet Atmospheres from Habitable to Lava Worlds Abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed rocky exoplanets far stranger than Earth and its Solar System siblings. The past three years have brought evidence for thick volatile atmospheres on the hottest lava worlds and bare surfaces on many of the coolest planets. I will briefly review how coupled interior-atmosphere mechanisms, from magma ocean outgassing to XUV-driven escape, shape rocky planet atmospheres in light of these observations. I will revisit the classical “cosmic shoreline,” anchored by Earth, Venus, and Mars, and share our recent findings recasting it as two boundaries set by distinct physics: an outgassing-regulated “cosmic sandbar” and an escape-regulated “cosmic shoreline” bounding an airless valley. item.title: Chris Dann — Building Dictatorships: Legitimacy & Large-Scale Infrastructure
item.description: Stanford Events — Contrary to expectations following the end of the Cold War, several autocracies have modernized without succumbing to democratizing pressures. This paper argues that a non-trivial number of 21st-century autocrats generate reputations for economic delivery via large-scale infrastructure due to its observability, tangibility, and durability as an asset, providing rulers with a credible commitment device for continued development while retaining authoritarian political institutions. I evaluate a central implication of this argument using geolocated data on 150,000 large-scale construction projects since 2005 and micro-level attitudes from nine harmonized survey datasets, covering 2.5 million respondents across 2,300 subnational districts. Exploiting within-district variation, I find that effective project delivery increases perceived government performance, with effects concentrated among established autocracies and democratic backsliders. item.title: A Captured Field, an Open Contest: Serbia’s Upcoming Elections
item.description: Stanford Events — Serbia goes to the polls on October 25 in an early parliamentary election, called after nearly two years of sustained protest. A presidential election will follow by the end of December, after President Vučić resigned in September to run for prime minister. A list emerging from the student movement leads in independent polling, and most opposition parties have stepped back to support it. It will contest seats against a party that has, over the past decade, consolidated control over broadcast media, the security apparatus, electoral administration, the public sector and the regulatory bodies. The conditions are heavily uneven. National broadcasters and the tabloid press are aligned with the ruling party, while the regulatory bodies that might act as a corrective to this have repeatedly declined to act. Public funds, public employment and public contracts are used as leverage on voters. Questions about the accuracy of the voter register remain unresolved from previous cycles. Internation

item.title: Curator Led Talk | surfacing
item.description: Stanford Events — Join Kelsey Chen, Exhibition Co-Curator, on this special tour of surfacing. RSVP HERE patty chang: surfacing engages the ocean as a physical, geopolitical, and symbolic space. The exhibition culminates a year-long residency through the Denning Visiting Artist program, during which Chang was embedded at Stanford’s Hopkins Marine Station. Incorporating fish specimens, archaeological remains, archival materials documenting the lives of Chinese fisher families in the early 1900s, and a porcelain table that travels from the Metropolitan Museum of Art to take new form at the Anderson, Chang’s sculptural practice surfaces the mysterious intimacies and unrecorded histories that haunt the Pacific Ocean and its coast. surfacing is the first solo artist exhibition commission for Stanford’s Asian American Art Initiative (AAAI). The exhibition will be on view in the Wisch Family Gallery from September 17, 2026 – February 8, 2027. Location: Anderson Collection

item.title: eWEAR Seminar: The Quantified Self for Health
item.description: Stanford Events — Quantified self is a cultural trend of self-tracking that incorporates technology and data acquisition into daily life, often with the goal of improving physical and mental health or to improve performance. The widespread use of wearables that track fitness, health, and sleep have enabled more individuals who seek "self-knowledge through numbers” to engage in quantified self techniques for disease management and wellness. item.title: 36th Annual Jonathan J. King Lecture: Dr. Bryant Lin & Dr. Shoshana Ungerleider
item.description: Stanford Events — The Girand Center for Biomedical Ethics is pleased to announce this year’s speaker, Dr. Bryant Lin, in conversation with Dr. Shoshana Ungerleider, for the 36th Annual Jonathan J. King Lecture. We invite you to join us on Thursday, November 5 at 5:30pm PT in the Cedar Room at the Stanford Faculty Club or via livestream for My Cancer Journey: Happiness and Sadness, Hope and Fear. In this talk, Dr. Lin will share a candid and deeply personal reflection on living with terminal cancer. As a leading researcher, cancer advocate, and patient, he brings a rare perspective to the realities of serious illness, clinical care, hope, and what it means to live fully in the face of uncertainty. Joining Dr. Lin is Dr. Shoshana Ungerleider, a physician, journalist, producer, and leading voice in compassionate, patient-centered care.
